title: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
summary: What a process owns versus what a thread shares, how Linux builds both from clone(), what the kernel does during a switch, and why the cache and TLB refill afterwards usually costs more than the switch itself.
outcomes: Explain which state is private to a thread and which is shared by every thread of a process
Map fork() and pthread_create() to the clone() flags Linux uses for each
Trace a context switch from the timer interrupt through switch_to and back to user mode
Compute the CPU share lost to switching from a switch rate and a per-switch cost
Diagnose voluntary versus involuntary switch counts and choose a thread design to match

lessons.title: What a process owns and what a thread shares

blocks.md: From OS basics you know a **process** is a running program, and that the OS keeps each process's saved state in a **process control block (PCB)**. This course zooms into two questions that decide how fast concurrent software runs: what exactly is the difference between a process and a thread, and what does it cost to switch the CPU from one to another?

It helps to split a process into two parts.

- **Resources**: the address space (code, heap, globals, memory mappings), the open file descriptor table, the current working directory, and the table of signal handlers.
- **An execution stream**: a program counter (PC), the CPU registers, and a stack for function calls.

A **thread** is just an execution stream. A classic process has exactly one; a multi-threaded process has several, all sharing one set of resources.

OSTEP puts it this way: each thread is very much like a separate process, except that threads share the same address space. Each thread still needs its own saved registers, kept in a **thread control block (TCB)**, and its own stack, so a two-threaded process has two stacks in one address space. Local variables live on a thread's stack; globals and `malloc` memory are shared by every thread.

blocks.title: Threads share one process; fork makes a second process

nodes.label:
Process PID 100
memory, fds, cwd, handlers

Kernel scheduler
picks a runnable thread

scenes.caption: A single-threaded process: one execution stream (thread 1) plus one bundle of resources. The thread's own state is tiny: a program counter, registers and a stack.
pthread_create adds thread 2. It gets its own registers and stack but points at the same memory, file descriptors and signal handlers. A write to a global by either thread is seen by both.
fork() instead creates a new process: a new thread inside a new resource bundle that starts as a copy. After the fork, writes on one side are invisible to the other.
The scheduler runs threads, not processes. Here it has three runnable threads to place on CPUs, two of which happen to belong to the same process.

blocks.prompt: In the program below, a child process sets the global `x = 1`, then later a thread sets `x = 1`. What does the parent print each time?
blocks.reveal: The parent prints `x=0` after the fork and `x=1` after the thread. `fork()` gives the child a private copy of memory, so its write is invisible to the parent. A thread shares the parent's address space, so its write is the parent's write.

blocks.title: The same write, once from a child process, once from a thread

scenes.caption: The parent starts with x = 0 in its address space.
fork() returns 0 in the child, which sets x = 1. That write lands in the child's private copy of the page.
The parent waits for the child to exit, then prints its own x. The child's write never reached it.
Now a thread runs bump(). It shares the parent's address space, so x = 1 writes the very same memory the main thread reads.
Same instruction, different result: sharing is decided by what the new execution stream was given, not by the code it runs.
scenes.output:
after fork: x=0
after thread: x=1

blocks.md: A process is a **resource container** (memory, files, handlers); a thread is an **execution stream** (PC, registers, stack). Threads in one process see each other's writes; separate processes do not, unless they set up sharing on purpose.

Why have both? OSTEP gives two reasons to use threads: **parallelism** (one thread per CPU working on parts of a big job) and **overlapping I/O** (while one thread waits on disk or network, another computes). Threads make sharing data easy, which is also why shared data needs locks. Processes are the sounder choice for logically separate tasks that share little, since a bug or crash in one cannot scribble over the other's memory.

blocks.question: Thread A in a process opens a file and gets file descriptor 5. Thread B, in the same process, calls `read(5, buf, 100)` without opening anything. What happens?
options: It fails with EBADF, because descriptors are private to the thread that opened them
It reads from the same open file, because threads share the process's descriptor table
It reads from a fresh copy of the file starting at offset 0
It blocks until thread A closes the descriptor
blocks.explain: The descriptor table is a process resource, so every thread in the process sees fd 5 and the same file offset. Only per-thread state (registers, stack, signal mask, thread ID) is private.

blocks.question: A function stores a pointer to one of its local variables in a global, then returns. Another thread later dereferences that pointer. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: threads share the address space, so the local is still valid
The other thread cannot see the first thread's stack at all
The local lived on the first thread's stack frame, which was freed when the function returned, so the pointer now dangles
The kernel copies the local to the other thread's stack
blocks.explain: The memory is reachable (it is all one address space), but the stack frame is dead once the function returns and will be reused by later calls. Sharing the address space does not extend the lifetime of stack variables.

lessons.title: Linux: every thread is a task, and clone() picks what to share

blocks.md: Linux does not have separate kernel objects for processes and threads. Every schedulable entity is a **task** (a `struct task_struct` in the kernel), and new tasks are made by one system call, [`clone()`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/clone.2.html). Its flags say, resource by resource, whether the child **shares** the caller's resource or gets a **copy** of it.

The flags that matter most, from the clone(2) manual page:

- `CLONE_VM`: run in the same memory space; writes and `mmap` changes by one are seen by the other.
- `CLONE_FS`: share root directory, current working directory and umask.
- `CLONE_FILES`: share the file descriptor table.
- `CLONE_SIGHAND`: share the table of signal handlers.
- `CLONE_THREAD`: put the child in the caller's **thread group**.

blocks.title: clone() flags decide what the new task shares

scenes.caption: Five of the flags, by what they share: memory (VM), cwd, root and umask (FS), the descriptor table (FILES), signal handlers (SIGHAND, shown as SIGHND), and membership in the caller's thread group (THREAD).
glibc's fork() passes none of these flags, only SIGCHLD plus TID bookkeeping. Every resource is copied and the child starts a new thread group, so it gets its own PID.
glibc's pthread_create passes all five (plus SYSVSEM, SETTLS and TID flags). The new task shares everything and joins the caller's thread group, so getpid() returns the same value in both.
Other mixes are legal: CLONE_VM alone gives a separate process (own PID, own descriptors) that shares memory. But THREAD without SIGHAND fails with EINVAL, and SIGHAND requires VM.

blocks.caption: The only real difference between a thread and a forked process in glibc is this flag word. CLONE_SETTLS points the new thread at its own thread-local storage.

blocks.md: A **thread group** is how Linux implements the POSIX idea that all threads of a process share one PID. The shared PID is the **thread group ID (TGID)**, and `getpid()` returns it. Each task also has a unique **thread ID (TID)**, returned by `gettid()`. The first thread's TID equals the TGID. Tools such as `ps -L`, or the directory `/proc/PID/task/`, list every thread of a process.

glibc's threading library (NPTL) is a **1:1** implementation: the [pthreads(7)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/pthreads.7.html) page says each thread maps to a kernel scheduling entity, created with `clone()`, and that mutexes and joins are built on the `futex()` system call. So every pthread is scheduled, preempted and context-switched by the kernel exactly like a process.

Misconception: "threads are cheap because the kernel treats them as lighter objects." On Linux a thread and a process are the same kind of task. A thread is cheaper to create because there is less to set up (no new address space or page tables), and switching between two threads of one process is cheaper because the address space stays loaded. Those savings come from sharing, not from a different kind of object.

What about the cost of `fork()` for a big process? The fork(2) page notes that Linux uses **copy-on-write** pages, so the only cost is duplicating the parent's page tables and creating a task structure for the child. OSTEP describes the trick: map the same physical page into both address spaces read-only, and copy a page only when someone writes to it.

blocks.title: Copy-on-write fork: copy page tables, not pages

scenes.caption: Before fork: the parent maps virtual pages 0 to 3 to physical frames 7, 8, 9 and 12, all writable. (Frame numbers are illustrative.)
fork() copies only the page table entries. Both processes now point at the same four frames, and the kernel marks every entry read-only in both.
The child writes to page 2. The read-only entry causes a page fault; the kernel sees a copy-on-write page, copies frame 9 into a new frame 20 and maps it writable for the child only.
Only one page was copied. If the child now calls exec(), its whole address space is replaced and the other three shared pages were never copied at all.

blocks.md: Put numbers on it. A process with 1 GiB of memory in 4 KiB pages has $2^{30}/2^{12} = 262{,}144$ pages. With 8-byte page table entries (as on x86-64), the last level of its page tables is $262{,}144 \times 8$ bytes $= 2$ MiB. So fork copies about 2 MiB of entries instead of 1 GiB of data, 512 times less, and then pays one page copy per page actually written. (Simplified: upper levels of the page table are tiny, and some mappings need no copying at all.)

blocks.question: A thread in a 4-thread web server calls `chdir("/tmp")`, then another thread opens the relative path `log.txt`. Where does the file get opened?
options: In /tmp, because pthreads share CLONE_FS state such as the working directory
In the old working directory, because each thread keeps its own cwd
It depends on which CPU each thread runs on
The open fails because cwd changes are not allowed in multi-threaded programs
blocks.explain: pthread_create passes CLONE_FS, so the working directory is shared by all threads of the process. This is a real source of bugs: a library that calls chdir silently changes path resolution for every thread.

blocks.question: A 16 GiB database process calls `fork()` to take a snapshot, and the child only reads memory and writes it to disk while the parent keeps serving writes. Which cost grows over time?
options: None: copy-on-write means fork never copies data
The child's reads, because reading a shared page triggers a copy
The parent's writes: each first write to a still-shared page faults and copies that page, so memory use grows with the number of distinct pages the parent modifies
The initial fork, which copies all 16 GiB before returning
blocks.explain: Reads of shared pages are free. Each page the parent modifies while the child still maps it must be copied once, so both memory use and page-fault work grow with the parent's write set during the snapshot.

lessons.title: Anatomy of a context switch, step by step

blocks.md:
A **context switch** stops the thread running on a CPU, saves enough of its state to resume it later, and resumes a different thread. You already know the trigger mechanism from limited direct execution: the kernel only gets control on a system call, an exception or an interrupt. That gives two kinds of switch:

- **Voluntary**: the thread gives up the CPU before its time slice ends, usually to wait for a resource (a read on an empty pipe, a contended lock, `sleep`).
- **Involuntary** (preemption): a higher-priority task became runnable or the thread used up its time slice, typically noticed on a timer interrupt.

The getrusage(2) page defines exactly these two counters (`ru_nvcsw` and `ru_nivcsw`), and Linux exposes them per thread as `voluntary_ctxt_switches` and `nonvoluntary_ctxt_switches` in `/proc/PID/status`. We will use them in the last lesson.

A switch saves state in two places. When the trap happens, A's user registers are saved on A's **kernel stack** (every thread has one, used while the kernel runs on its behalf). In OSTEP's model the **hardware** does it; on x86-64 the CPU pushes the user instruction pointer, stack pointer and flags, and the kernel entry code pushes the rest. Later, the kernel's switch routine saves A's *kernel* registers and loads B's; on Linux they go on A's kernel stack and only the stack pointer is stored in A's task structure. OSTEP's Figure 6.3 shows this protocol; the figure below follows it, with Linux names added.

blocks.title: A preemptive switch from thread A to thread B, and back

scenes.caption: Thread A is running user code. The timer interrupt fires, as set up by limited direct execution.
The hardware saves A's user registers onto A's kernel stack, switches to kernel mode and jumps to the interrupt handler.
The scheduler decides A has used its slice and picks B. If B is in a different process, the kernel also loads B's page table (on x86, a write to CR3).
switch_to pushes A's kernel registers onto A's kernel stack, stores A's stack pointer in A's task struct and loads B's. From now on the kernel is running on B's kernel stack.
Return-from-trap pops B's user registers off B's kernel stack and resumes B exactly where it was interrupted earlier. This was an involuntary switch for A.
Later B calls read() on an empty pipe. It cannot continue, so it gives up the CPU: a voluntary switch. The same save and restore steps run in the other direction.

blocks.prompt: Look at the assembly below. After `movq TASK_threadsp(%rsi), %rsp` loads B's stack pointer, the code pops six registers. Whose values do those pops restore: A's, which were just pushed, or B's?
blocks.reveal: **B's.** The pushes went onto A's stack; the pops read from B's stack, where B's registers were pushed the last time B itself ran this same code. The switch is the single instruction that changes `rsp`. Everything before it freezes A; everything after it thaws B. That is why the routine looks like it undoes itself but does not.

blocks.title: Linux x86-64 __switch_to_asm, simplified
blocks.code:
# rdi = prev task (A), rsi = next task (B)
__switch_to_asm:
    pushq %rbp        # save A's callee-saved
    pushq %rbx        # registers on A's
    pushq %r12        # kernel stack
    pushq %r13
    pushq %r14
    pushq %r15
    movq  %rsp, TASK_threadsp(%rdi)  # A.sp = rsp
    movq  TASK_threadsp(%rsi), %rsp  # rsp = B.sp
    popq  %r15        # these pops read B's
    popq  %r14        # stack, so they restore
    popq  %r13        # B's saved values
    popq  %r12
    popq  %rbx
    popq  %rbp
    jmp   __switch_to # C part: FPU, TLS, current=B

scenes.caption: Entered from context_switch() on A's kernel stack. Addresses are illustrative: A's stack top is 0xA000, and B saved its stack pointer at 0xAFD0 when it was last switched out.
Six pushes save A's callee-saved registers. Each is 8 bytes, so rsp drops by 48 bytes to 0x9FD0.
Save A's stack pointer into A's task struct. A is now frozen: everything needed to resume it is on its kernel stack plus this one pointer.
The actual switch is a single instruction: load B's saved stack pointer. The CPU is now on B's kernel stack.
scenes.output: now running on B's kernel stack

scenes.caption: The pops mirror the pushes, but they read B's stack, so they restore the values B pushed when it was switched out. rsp climbs back by 48 bytes to 0xB000.
__switch_to (C) saves A's FPU state, loads B's thread-local storage base and sets current to B. Its final ret pops B's return address, so B resumes inside its own earlier call to the scheduler.
scenes.output:
now running on B's kernel stack
return into B's context_switch()

blocks.md: Linux saves only the **callee-saved** registers here because `switch_to` is called like a normal function: the C calling convention already lets it clobber the others. The x86-64 path then continues in `__switch_to`, which saves A's floating-point and vector (FPU) registers and arranges for B's to be reloaded before B returns to user mode, loads B's thread-local storage base, and updates the per-CPU `current` pointer. OSTEP's Figure 6.4 shows the same idea in xv6's 32-bit `swtch` routine.

blocks.title: The Linux switch path: what is skipped for threads

scenes.caption: Every switch goes through context_switch() in kernel/sched/core.c. It first deals with the address space (mm), then calls switch_to for registers and the stack.
Thread to thread in the same process: switch_mm_irqs_off sees the same mm already loaded and returns early. The x86 source comments: no TLB flush required.
Process to process: the kernel writes the new page table root into CR3, applies process-to-process speculation mitigations if enabled, and may need to flush TLB entries.
Switching to a kernel thread (no user memory): it borrows the previous task's address space instead of loading one, called lazy TLB mode. No page table switch at all.

blocks.md: Register save and restore is the same for every switch. The difference between a thread switch and a process switch is the address space: if `next` shares `prev`'s memory, the page table stays loaded and the TLB stays valid.

blocks.question: Two threads of the same process alternate on one CPU. Compared with two separate processes alternating, which step does the kernel skip?
options: Saving and restoring the general-purpose registers
Switching kernel stacks
Loading a new page table root (CR3 on x86) and the TLB work that comes with it
Running the scheduler to pick the next task
blocks.explain: Each thread still has its own registers and kernel stack, so those are always swapped, and the scheduler always runs. Only the address space is shared, so switch_mm finds the same mm and returns without touching CR3.

blocks.question: A thread calls `pthread_mutex_lock` on a lock another thread holds, and it sleeps until the lock is free. How is this counted?
options: As an involuntary switch, because the thread did not want to stop
As a voluntary switch, because it gave up the CPU before its slice ended to wait for a resource
It is not a context switch, because the lock is in user space
As a system call but not a switch
blocks.explain: Blocking on anything (I/O, a futex-based lock, sleep) is a voluntary switch in the getrusage sense: the thread released the CPU early. Involuntary means it was preempted while it still wanted to run.

lessons.title: What a switch really costs: direct work and cold caches

blocks.md: The **direct cost** of a switch is the work the kernel does every time: enter the kernel, run the scheduler, save and restore registers, possibly load a new page table, and return. OSTEP reports lmbench measurements from 1996: on a 200 MHz P6 running Linux 1.3.37, a system call took about 4 microseconds and a context switch about 6. It adds that modern 2 to 3 GHz machines are almost an order of magnitude faster, with sub-microsecond results.

How do you measure something that short? Ousterhout's trick (1990), later used by lmbench, is a **pipe ping-pong**: pin two processes to the same CPU, connect them with two pipes, and pass one byte back and forth. Each process blocks on `read` until the other writes, so every hop forces a switch. Li, Ding and Shen (2007) subtract the system-call work by also timing one process that writes and reads one pipe to itself, which does the same calls with no switch.

blocks.caption: t1: 10,000 real round trips (20,000 switches, each paired with one read and one write). t2: 10,000 simulated round trips (one read plus one write each, no switch).

blocks.md: Worked example with illustrative timings: if the 10,000 real round trips take $t_1 = 120$ ms and the 10,000 simulated ones take $t_2 = 22$ ms, then each real hop costs $120\text{ ms}/20000 = 6$ microseconds, of which $22\text{ ms}/10000 = 2.2$ microseconds is the read and write. That leaves $c_1 = 3.8$ microseconds for the switch itself, which happens to be the value the paper measured.

The bigger cost is **indirect**. The incoming thread finds caches, TLB and branch predictors full of the previous thread's state, so its first stretch of work runs slowly while it refills them. Li et al. measured the **total** cost $c_2$ by having each process sweep an array between switches, and estimate the indirect part as $c_2 - c_1$.

blocks.title: Cost per switch measured by Li, Ding and Shen (2007)

scenes.caption: Direct cost with processes that touch no data: 3.8 microseconds on a 2.0 GHz Xeon running Linux 2.6.17.
Each process now sweeps an array between switches. While everything fits in the 512 KB L2 cache, the total stays between 4.2 and 8.7 microseconds.
Arrays of 256 KB to 512 KB: one process alone fits in L2 but the two together do not, so each switch means refilling the cache. Cost rises from 38.6 to 203.2 microseconds.
Arrays too big for the cache, swept with a 128-byte stride that defeats the prefetcher: a mean of 825.3 microseconds per switch (8-byte stride: 116.5). Direct cost is now under 1 percent.

blocks.md: Misconception: "a context switch costs a few microseconds, so it does not matter." That is the direct cost on an idle cache. Li et al. found the total ranged from several microseconds to more than a thousand, depending on working set size and access pattern. Benchmarks that touch no data hide the part that hurts.

The TLB is a special case of the same problem. Translations cached for one address space are meaningless for another. OSTEP describes two fixes: **flush the TLB** on every process switch, or tag each entry with an **address space identifier (ASID)** so entries from several processes coexist. Threads of one process share an address space, so switching between them needs neither.

blocks.title: Why tagged TLB entries survive a process switch

scenes.caption: P1 runs and its virtual page 10 maps to physical frame 100 (OSTEP's example). The TLB caches that translation.
Switch to P2, whose page 10 maps to frame 170. With untagged entries the TLB cannot tell whose 10 is whose, so the switch flushes it. P2 starts by missing.
P2 walks its page table and refills. When P1 runs again it will miss on everything it used before: that refill work is part of the switch's real cost.
Now with address space identifiers. Each entry carries the ASID of its owner, so both translations of page 10 can live in the TLB at once and nothing is flushed.
Back to P1 (ASID 1): its lookup of page 10 matches entry 0 and hits immediately. Linux on x86 calls this PCID and keeps a few recent address spaces tagged per CPU.

blocks.md: On x86 the tag is the **PCID**. Rather than giving every process a permanent tag, Linux keeps a small per-CPU array caching the last few address spaces that ran there (6, set by `TLB_NR_DYN_ASIDS` in `arch/x86/include/asm/tlbflush.h`), so switching back to a recently run process can skip the flush. Process switches can also trigger speculative-execution mitigations that thread switches skip, which widens the gap further.

blocks.prompt: A service handles 10,000 requests per second on one core, and each request moves between two threads via a queue, causing 2 switches. If each switch costs 3.8 microseconds directly plus a cache refill that brings the total to about 38.6 microseconds, how much of the core goes to switching?
blocks.reveal: $20{,}000$ switches per second $\times$ $38.6$ microseconds $= 0.772$ seconds per second, so about **77 percent** of the core. Counting only the 3.8 microsecond direct cost would suggest 7.6 percent. Handing every request between threads is a design choice with a real price.

blocks.title: Share of a core lost to switching

x.label: context switches per second per core

params.name: c
params.label: cost per switch incl. cache refill (us)

scenes.caption: Simplified model: lost fraction = switches per second x cost per switch. At 10,000 switches per second, 3.8 microseconds each costs 3.8 percent of a core.
With a cache refill of the size measured for 256 KB working sets (38.6 us total), the same 10,000 switches per second cost 38.6 percent.
With 203.2 us per switch, even 1,000 switches per second cost 20.3 percent. The indirect cost, not the register save, decides whether switching hurts.

blocks.question: You benchmark a context switch with a ping-pong of two processes that touch no memory, and get 2 microseconds. Your real service switches 5,000 times a second between processes with 400 KB working sets on a CPU with a 512 KB cache. What should you expect?
options: About 1 percent overhead, since 5,000 x 2 us = 10 ms per second
No overhead, since the working sets fit in cache
Noticeably more than 1 percent, because each switch also refills cache the other process evicted, and the benchmark measured none of that
Less than 1 percent, because larger working sets amortize the switch
blocks.explain: Two 400 KB working sets do not fit in a 512 KB cache together, the regime where Li et al. saw tens to hundreds of microseconds per switch. The empty ping-pong measures only the direct cost.

blocks.question: Why is switching between two threads of the same process usually cheaper than between two processes, even though both save and restore the same registers?
options: Threads have fewer registers
The address space stays loaded, so there is no page table switch, no TLB flush and the shared code and data may still be in cache
The kernel does not run the scheduler for threads
Thread switches happen entirely in user space on Linux
blocks.explain: With NPTL's 1:1 model the kernel schedules threads like any task, so the scheduler and register work are the same. The saving is the address space: no CR3 write, valid TLB entries, and shared data that may still be warm.

lessons.title: Counting switches and designing around them

blocks.md: You cannot optimize what you do not count. Linux keeps two counters per thread: `/proc/PID/task/TID/status` shows each thread's, and `/proc/PID/status` shows the main thread's only, and `getrusage()` reports the same split for the whole process:

blocks.caption: ru_nvcsw counts voluntary switches, ru_nivcsw involuntary ones.

blocks.md:
The two counters point at different problems:

- **Many involuntary switches**: threads are being preempted while they still want to run, so there are more runnable threads than cores. Check whether CPU-bound work is spread over far more threads than cores, or whether noisy neighbours share the machine.
- **Many voluntary switches**: threads keep blocking. That is healthy for I/O, but a high rate on CPU-bound code often means lock contention or fine-grained handoffs between threads through queues.

blocks.title: Same work, different numbers of threads, on two cores

scenes.caption: Four CPU-bound jobs of 6 ms each, run by a pool of 2 worker threads (one per core) taking jobs from a queue. Jobs finish at 6, 12, 6 and 12 ms: mean 9 ms, zero switches between workers.

One thread per job instead, with a 3 ms time slice (simplified round robin). Each core switches 3 times, 6 involuntary switches in all. Jobs finish at 9, 12, 9 and 12 ms: mean 10.5 ms. Same total work, later answers.

At ms-scale slices the direct cost is tiny (3 switches x 3.8 us is under 0.1 percent of 12 ms). The real losses are later completions and, if working sets collide in cache, refill time after each switch.
Where switches pay off: T1 computes 2 ms, then blocks on a 4 ms disk read. The voluntary switch lets T2 use the core meanwhile, so the core never idles.

blocks.md: Misconception: "more threads means more parallelism." Parallelism is capped by the number of cores. Past that, extra CPU-bound threads only take turns: they add involuntary switches, push answers later, and make threads evict each other's cache. Extra threads help only when they spend time blocked, as in the I/O scene.

Common designs follow from the cost model:

1. **Size CPU pools to cores.** A worker pool with about one thread per core keeps involuntary switches near zero for CPU-bound work.
2. **Do not hand off per item.** Passing every request between threads costs two switches each; batching, or letting one thread carry a request to completion, removes them.
3. **Multiplex I/O on few threads.** Event loops (epoll, io_uring) let one thread wait for thousands of sockets, so blocking does not require one thread per connection.
4. **Pin threads** with `sched_setaffinity()` when cache warmth matters; context-switch benchmarks such as lmbench also keep both processes on one CPU, but for another reason: so every hop is a real switch on that CPU.

Some runtimes go further and switch in user space. Go's scheduler multiplexes many goroutines (G) onto worker threads (M), each needing a processor slot (P) to run Go code, as the comment at the top of [runtime/proc.go](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/master/src/runtime/proc.go) describes. Switching goroutines on the same thread needs no kernel entry, so the direct cost shrinks. The indirect cost does not vanish: a different goroutine still brings different data into the cache.

The one number to remember is not the microseconds of a single switch but **switches per second times total cost per switch**, where total includes the cache and TLB refill. Keep CPU-bound threads near the core count, and reserve extra threads or async I/O for work that actually waits.

blocks.question: A CPU-bound image service runs 64 worker threads on an 8-core machine. `nonvoluntary_ctxt_switches` climbs by thousands per second per thread, and p99 latency is high even though CPU is at 100 percent. What is the best first change?
options: Add more worker threads so each request is more likely to find one free
Cut the pool to about 8 workers and queue requests, so each runs to completion on a core
Raise the time slice so involuntary switches become voluntary
Move the workers into separate processes for isolation
blocks.explain: There are 8 times more runnable threads than cores, so threads keep preempting each other: high involuntary counts and late completions, as in the timeline. A core-sized pool with a queue removes most switches. Processes would make each switch more expensive, not rarer.

blocks.question: A logging thread receives each log line from 16 worker threads through a mutex-protected queue and is woken for every line. At 200,000 lines per second, `voluntary_ctxt_switches` on the logger is enormous. Which fix targets the cause?
options: Give the logger a higher scheduling priority
Use more logging threads, one per worker
Batch: let workers append to a buffer and wake the logger once per batch (or every few milliseconds) instead of per line
Pin the logger to core 0
blocks.explain: Each line wakes the logger, which handles it and sleeps again: one voluntary switch per line on the logger, plus wakeup work for the workers. Batching turns 200,000 handoffs into a few hundred. More logging threads multiply the switches, and priority or pinning do not change how often they happen.

blocks.question: Which workload benefits most from running more threads than cores?
options: Matrix multiplication that never blocks
A crawler where each request spends 95 percent of its time waiting on the network
A compression job reading from a RAM disk
A tight spin loop measuring time
blocks.explain: Threads that mostly wait free the core through voluntary switches, so extra threads overlap waiting with useful work. CPU-bound jobs gain nothing beyond the core count. (An event loop is the other way to get the same overlap with fewer threads.)
